statement: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 10 and BC = 6. Point P can be anywhere on side AB. What is the area of triangle PCD?

choices.misconception: I placed P at the middle of AB, used half of AB, 5, as the base with height 6, and halved.
I worked out the perimeter of the rectangle, 2 x (10 + 6), instead of an area.
I multiplied the base CD by the height 6 and forgot to halve for a triangle.

choices.text: It depends on where P is
choices.misconception: I assumed moving P along AB changes the area, without noticing that its height above CD never changes.

hints: Sketch it and choose side CD as the base.
With CD as the base, the height is the distance from P to the line CD. Ask whether that distance changes as P slides along AB, which is parallel to CD.
The base CD is 10 and the height is always BC = 6, so the area is half of 10 x 6.

solutions.reliable: Draw the rectangle with AB on top and CD at the bottom. Take CD, of length 10, as the base of triangle PCD. Since P lies on AB, which is parallel to CD, its distance from CD is always 6. So the area is (1/2) x 10 x 6 = 30, wherever P is. The transferable idea: draw the diagram and choose the base whose height you know, especially when a point is allowed to move.
solutions.elegant: Slide P to corner A: triangle ACD is exactly half the rectangle, 60 / 2 = 30. Since the height of P above CD never changes, every position gives the same answer.

whyOnTest: Drawing the figure shows the height is fixed, which turns an apparently underdetermined question into a one-line area calculation.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
